recentItems.title: The Greatest Cadenza I Ever Heard
recentItems.description:
I knew John Sauer when we were both Antioch students in the early '70s. He was -- and still is -- a brilliant pianist who never took his extraordinary talent seriously unless he had to for concerts and private audition recordings for others that I was tasked to tape.

Before the "proper" recordings for those auditions, John would play joke pieces he'd make up on the spot, parodying snarky television ads and silly childrens tunes, playing them straight until he entered a dark zone, and the tunes would suddenly turn into something far more sinister. All spontaneous, all effortless and, as I said, all brilliant.

Because of the student strike that shut the campus down for most of the Spring '73 quarter, music faculty members David Stock and John Ronsheim organized a concert at Wittenberg University, located a few miles north in Springfield, on May 24. David would be conducting his student orchestra (and his wife who was part of the 1st Violin section), and John would be directing his student chorus.

The highlights began after the intermission when John's chorus sang Dufay's M. Ave Regina Caelorum -- this was partly in preparation for the chorus's European tour a month later -- and David conducted Bach's Fifth Brandenburg Concerto.

I recorded both the Dufay and Bach that night. 

The Bach concerto featured a stunningly difficult cadenza -- an extended keyboard solo near the end of the first movement where the tempo would hold steady in 4th gear but then shift to an unthinkable 10th, then slowing back down to 4th until the orchestra returned.

And John Sauer was going to play it.

Everyone who knew John didn't know what to expect. Was he adequately prepared? Would he mess up? Was this going to work? We were all at the edge of our seats with every note he played, watching to see what would happen, especially when we had a suspicion that he was sight-reading the score.

Keep in mind: We're not looking at perfection here; we're looking at survival.

I'm not sure if that tension can be sensed by those who weren't there and listening to it now over half a century later. But for me, it's still felt, this high-wire act without a net and then coming out whole again on the other side.

For me, it still remains a wonder.

The cadenza begins here soon after the 7-minute mark. Excuse the crude video; there was very little with which to work.

recentItems.title: Ockeghem Choir of San Francisco, 1978: Ockeghem's "Petite Camusette"
recentItems.description:
The remaining piece from our last performance at St. Mark's Episcopal Church in Berkeley, California, on April 21, 1978. "Petite Camusette" is a secular work, here rendered by a small chorus rather than by soloists and/or instruments, because we felt it best captured the full impact of Ockeghem's music.

As always, dedicated to the memory of John Ronsheim, music professor at Antioch College from 1967 to 1990, who injected all of his students with his love for this extraordinary composer. A Ronsheim biography is forthcoming.

Sopranos: Diana Dillaway, Diana Rogers, Kyle Rudnick
Altos: Catherine Bauman, Rachel Levin, Lyle York
Tenors: Doug Goodkin, Ken Gundry, Tad Merrick, Peter Sorensen
Basses: Scott Horton, Dick Illig, Peter Kohn
Director: Don Giller

Ronsheim photo by Ryck Lent, Fall 1972

recentItems.title: Carson, Letterman, and Malkoff
recentItems.description:
Mark Malkoff is publishing a book on Johnny Carson, with a special focus on his 30-year run hosting "The Tonight Show." Its release date is October 21, 2025, two days before the centennial of Johnny's birth.

If there's anyone best qualified for such a task, it's Mark. For eight years, he hosted nearly 400 episodes of "The Carson Podcast," talking with hundreds of Johnny's guests and staffers, gaining invaluable insights into every aspect of Johnny's television career.

Soon after ending his podcast series, Mark devoted four years collecting all of his podcast data and interviewing yet more people, constructing perhaps _the_ definitive behind-the-scenes look at television's most successful and impactful talk show of its time.

I had a chance to read his pre-release version, and it's nothing short of spectacular. There are stories that have never been revealed before, including David Letterman's first guest appearance and Joan Rivers' feud with Johnny. I can't praise Mark's work enough.

Mark asked me to help promote his book, and I'm happy to do so here. Among the many outlets the book is being sold, here's the Amazon link: https://a.co/d/06loIF1

Every fan of Johnny Carson -- every fan of late night television --  will want to read this book.

(Upload granted by Worldwide Pants, Inc.)

recentItems.title: Ockeghem Choir of San Franciscoi, 1978: Ave Maria
recentItems.description:
Another selection from The Ockeghem Choir of San Francisco's final concert on April 21, 1978. This is one of Ockeghem's sublime motets, "Ave Maria" for four voices.

John Ronsheim, the Antioch College music professor who injected Ockeghem into our veins, never worked on this motet. He did, however, mark up the transcription I had sent him at around the same time, so perhaps he had considered it.

As with all of Ockeghem's works, this is more difficult to perform than it might appear. But I'm pleased with its presentation, especially after hearing other online versions.

I added in the dim background a portion of a 2015 dance piece choreographed by one of John's granddaughters, Celeste Patten, eighteen years after John had passed in 1997. The piece's original soundtrack came from a String Trio John had composed while a graduate student at the New England Conservatory of Music in 1953.

The two folios in the Chigi manuscript that includes "Ave Maria" courtesy of DVL Digivatlib.

Sopranos: Diana Dillaway, Diana Rogers, Kyle Rolnick
Altos: Catherine Bauman, Rachel Levin, Lyle York
Tenors: Doug Goodkin, Ken Gundry, Tad Merrick (RIP), Peter Sorensen
Basses: Scott Horton, Dick Illig, Peter Kohn
Director: Don Giller

recentItems.title: Tad Lathrop and Don Giller, "City Lights" (1977, 2004)
recentItems.description:
Tad brought this tune to my apartment one night in July 1977 when we were both living in San Francisco. We recorded our electric guitar parts and his first vocals onto my sound-on-sound reel-to-reel tape deck. We then overdubbed his second vocals and my momentary harmonies. The music was finished, the lyrics not, so Tad just repeated the first verse for the second.

From there the song sat for the next 27 years.

In 2004, when I was working on tracks that would end up on our 2006 CD "Red Horizon," we decided to re-record "City Lights" from scratch. Tad, back in SF after living in NYC throughout much of the '80s, recorded his electric guitars and basic drum parts and then sent them to me; I had moved to NYC in 1978.

He then completed his lyrics and sang a few takes, all preserved in his digital files, and he sent them to me as well.

I then added everything else -- a multi-track percussion section, a couple acoustic guitars, a couple electric guitars at the Coda, a bass, and some background vocals.

There are some neat musical ideas hidden in there -- guitars that travel in opposite directions within the chorus but tonally appropriate, anticipatory background vocals, and combinations of Tad's various vocal takes. I always liked the song itself, and I hope we did it justice.

The photos are by Tad Lathrop, Kevin Lathrop, and the cities-at-night collection at unsplash.com.

Photographers in the order of photo depiction: Tad Lathrop, Tad Lathrop, Tad Lathrop, Kevin Lathrop, Igor Karimov, Amber Kipp, Tejiri Ibihwiori, Phil Hauser, Nono, Hiep Duong, Ivan Benets, Tad Lathrop, Tad Lathrop, Arthur Tseng, Platon Matakaev, Antonino Visalli, Jonas Verstuyft, Raymond Kotewicz, Jake Weirick, Mykhailo Amirdzhanian, Dongsh, Benjamin Sow, Tian Zhang, Tiffany Bernarte

recentItems.title: Tad Lathrop and Don Giller: Home Demos, 1972-1984
recentItems.description:
This is a collection of home demos Tad and I had recorded either alone or together from 1972 until 1984. Five are instrumentals, two include vocals.

Most are complete compositions we would record solely to preserve their existence. Also included are some early run-throughs before we were satisfied with the songs' constructions.

The video here is sparse, no visual distractions. Just the music.

1. Jackie, 1978 (Tad only, two guitars)
This was one of the fruits of Tad's mentorship with jazz guitarist extraordinaire Dave Creamer in San Francisco in the late '70s/early '80s. Tad's melodic and chordal strengths are at their peak here.

2. Love Is Easy, November 28, 1972.
An early Tad vocal composition that we recorded in my college dorm at Antioch in Yellow Springs, Ohio, the evening before we performed it and other songs of ours in concert.

3. Margo's Theme, 1983 and 1984
Another work of Tad's. Two versions: I recorded Tad going through an acoustic run-through in my NYC apartment on September 7, 1983, as I would eventually figure out what I should play during the song's bridge.
The second version is our completed arrangement, again recorded at my place a year later on November 16, 1984. I would later add snippets of Tad's playing from subsequent recordings at Tad's place in Brooklyn. We included this on our 2006 CD, "Red Horizon."

4. Sparky's Theme, 1975 and 1984
A piece of mine that I had been working on for nearly a decade.  Again, two versions: The first is me playing the main theme but coming up against a roadblock on what should follow. Recorded October 25, 1975, in my San Francisco apartment.
The second version has the song coming to completion with the roadblock lifted, thanks to Tad's exquisite counterpoint. Recorded in my NYC apartment on October 18, 1984.

5. Night Will Find a Way, 1978/79, 2003
Tad recorded this song of his in San Francisco in either 1978 or '79, overdubbing a harmonica over his guitar and vocal. I then added a guitar part in my NYC apartment on April 25, 2003. No sonic enhancements.

6. Tad's Song, May 18, 1974
Tad was about to leave San Francisco for points East, but before he left he recorded this in a warehouse converted into an artists' community called Project One.

7. Watermelon, February 24 and November 28, 1972
A work by Leo Kottke. Two versions: The first was one of the first pieces we had recorded together, here on February 24, 1972, in a different college dorm room of mine. Recently unearthed, I felt it had a warmer, softer tone than the second version from the same evening we had recorded "Love Is Easy" nine months later on November 28.
In that second version, we were more confident, the arrangement slightly different from the earlier one. Except for a botched ending on my part, this was a stronger, tighter performance though not as intimate as the first version.

All music but “Watermelon” Copyright ©️ Stomp-on-Henry Productions and Decent Interval Music.

recentItems.title: The Letterman Faces Project, Part 2: 1993–2015
recentItems.description:
“Sure, I like the Faces thing. Go nuts!”
— W.K., January 30, 2025

In commemoration of the 10th anniversary of Dave's final network broadcast. I'm presenting it now because reasons.

4,214. That's the number of Late Shows Dave hosted between August 30, 1993, and May 20, 2015. Every one of them is represented here in chronological order with a screen capture of Dave sitting behind his desk (or, in some instances, on a deskless chair when the show went to different one-off locations), looking directly at the camera. Not as tedious as one might imagine. More like mind- and eye-numbing.

And oh, the challenges with video aspect ratios that consumed eight Late Show years, and the songs editing (a few performances came from multiple show sources, one even from Late Night), details with which I won't burden you. One song was edited together and added at the last minute because I needed 1 minute and 8 seconds to fill.

Yes, there are more than a few color issues, particularly during the early years, but life is short, and it may be a surprise to some that I do actually have one.

Many of the soundtrack selections come from the show's commercial breaks, until now heard only by those in the Sullivan Theatre, and most have special meanings for Paul, Dave, and the show. The coda has a special meaning for many more.

Be advised that it's 33-and-a-half minutes you'll never get back. Count the ties!

Great, great thanks to Walter Kim at Worldwide Pants for letting me do this. It's a long-delayed sequel to Faces, Part 1, which comprised the Late Night years.

recentItems.title: John Richard Ronsheim (1927–1997), A Life in Music and Photos - Revised
recentItems.description:
This is a revised video tribute to an extraordinary music professor I was fortunate to know when I attended Antioch College in Yellow Springs, Ohio, from 1969 until 1973.

All of the music selected here were staples in John's music courses except for his own composition, "Easter - Wings," and the two choral performances:

1. Louis Moreau Gottschalk - "The Banjo" Op. 15 (1853)
2. Charles Ives - "Decoration Day" (1912)
3. John Ronsheim - "Easter - Wings" (1964)
4. Charlie Parker - "Ko-Ko" (1946)
5. Richard Wagner - Love Duet from "Tristan & Isolde" (1865)
6. Francesco Landini - "Gran Pianto Agli Occhi" (Trecento)
7. Luigi Dallapiccola - "Ulisse" (1960-68)
8. Johannes Ockeghem - "Requiem" (15th C.)
9. Johannes Ockeghem - "M. Mi Mi" (15th C.)
10. Charlie Ives - "Charlie Rutlage" (1920-21)

The photos come from a number of sources -- yearbooks, friends, and other students. The batch from 1971 were taken by fellow Antioch student Andy Friedman. The two photos of the woman is his wife Eileen Stitz Ronsheim. The last photo of John is one I took the last time I saw him in early August 1978. They all have enormous meaning to those who knew him, and I hope others will begin to appreciate what a unique soul he was.

recentItems.title: Ockeghem Choir of San Francisco, 1977: Intemerata Dei Mater
recentItems.description:
Johannes Ockeghem's "Intemerata Dei Mater" motet consists of five voice parts, each their own fully-realized entity but when combined with the others form one of the densest compositions of the 15th century, no pauses in sight until the end of its three sections. Its contrapuntal richness and spiritual depth are unmatched within its time. It's also extremely difficult to perform.

Sharp ears will recognize the "Mi-Mi" motif in the lower voice at the very beginning.

All of the recordings of this piece on YouTube consist of soloists for each voice part. We tackled it with a 13-voice choir. We also performed it at a tempo two to three minutes faster than the other renditions, I feel more effectively capturing the intense rhythmic complexity of this masterpiece. We also adhered to what we believed was the original modal intent of the composer rather than more modern-day liberties with the ficta. For this performance we transposed it up a third to accommodate the singers' ranges.

As I discussed in previous Ockeghem Choir uploads, our aim was to present the beauty and spiritual fullness of the _music_ rather than highlighting individual soloists. For it's the music that matters above all else, a lesson John Ronsheim at Antioch had planted into our brains, and not the precious professionally-focused vocal (and dress) decorum of the singers.

As to the score: When transcribing this piece in 1976, I had little grasp of the proper positioning of ties and note stems. Seeing that professional music typesetting would become my livelihood nearly two decades later, one would think I'd know what I was doing back then. I clearly didn't.

Recorded live in concert at St. Mark's Episcopal Church in Berkeley, California, on February 19, 1977. The singers listed below are identified only within their four-part distribution. I have no memory how they were disbursed among five parts:

Soprano: Christine Powell, Carol Coan, Diana Rogers
Alto: Lyle York, Lynn Zinberg, Linda Hershovitz, Rachel Levin
Tenor: Tad Merrick (rip), Doug Goodkin, Bruce England
Bass: Peter Kohn, Scott Horton, Neil Goldstein

These are the finest people on the planet, and I cherish this period in my life with them.

Director: Don Giller

recentItems.title: Johannes Ockeghem, M. Mi-Mi (complete), Ockeghem Choir of San Francisco (1977)
recentItems.description:
This is a composite performance of Johannes Ockeghem's Missa Mi-Mi from two venues five days apart. The first is a run-through we recorded at St. Joseph's in Berkeley on February 24, 1977. By the time we got to the Sanctus, the group was pretty much drained, and the music suffered for it.

We held a concert at St. Mark's Episcopal Church, also in Berkeley, five days earlier on February 19. The first three mass movements -- Kyrie, Gloria, and Credo -- were a little dicey, but I feel it came together for the last two, the Sanctus and Agnus Dei.

So I've combined the two recordings: The Kyrie, Gloria, and Credo come from the run-through on February 24, while the Sanctus and Agnus Dei are from the live concert on February 19. The sonic dynamics between the two are apparent.

Also, we tended to drop around a half-step during the longer movements -- the Gloria and Credo -- and that becomes evident when we begin the Credo and Sanctus back on pitch.

This performance doesn't claim to be the definitive rendering of Ockeghem's stunning composition. Far from it. But it comes closer to the _music_ than the "professional" recordings out there. What we hear in those other performances are sterile settings with solo singers not blending together, focused only on their own voices. In our performance you hear the _music._ And it certainly isn't sterile.

Yes, there's the occasional awkward pitch, the occasional voice part not blending as tightly as it should. This is complicated music, and many of the approaching cadences are difficult to pull off with the complexity the contrapuntal moments present. And in one or two circumstances we miss the mark. But we pretty much got it everywhere else.

As to the mass: There's a century-long claim that its title is based on the E-A bass motif that begins each movement, the E being the "mi" of the "C" hexachord and the A the "mi" of the "F" hexachord. Only problem is that the "F" hexachord requires a Bb, and there is none in the signature.

Back in the mid-'70s, while transcribing this piece for the Choir, I realized that the mass was actually built on one of Ockeghem's chansons, "Presque transi," and I alluded to that in concert program notes at the time. Seems others have "discovered" that as well, decades later. Better late than never. Also that the text "My My," as it appears in the tenor voice in the mass's most authoritative source, the Chigi manuscript, as well as the iconography surrounding the  Kyrie folios, suggests that the setting may also be based on a pastoral play. But that's an essay for another day.

It's the music in the end. Those otherworldly duos. Those spectacularly dense cadences. Those sublime modal twists. And the end of the last Agnus: It's breathtaking. There's so much to love about this work. There's nothing like it.

The singers and bonding friends:
Sopranos: Christine Powell, Carol Coan, Diana Rogers
Altos: Lynn Zinberg, Linda Hershkovitz, Lyle York, Rachel Levin
Tenors: Doug Goodkin, Tad Merrick (RIP), Bruce England
Basses: Scott Horton, Peter Kohn, Neil Goldstein

Director: Don Giller
